A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Pyramid Attention Broadcast work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across appendix reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original video-quality measurements, latency comparisons, component ablations, and GPU-scaling experiments on Open-Sora, Open-Sora-Plan, and Latte.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds WebVid evaluation, long-scene tests, detailed profiling, redundancy analyses, and FLUX results.

M1.justification: The attention-output broadcasting procedure, differentiated broadcast ranges, and broadcast sequence parallelism remain unchanged. MLP broadcasting already appears in v1's introduction and Table 2; v2 documents its configuration and rationale. The FLUX experiment applies the existing strategy without establishing a new algorithmic component.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained VBench video experiments, v2 adds evaluation on 1,000 WebVid videos (Appendix B.1), a targeted complex/dynamic-scene scenario using 16-second Open-Sora videos (B.3), and text-to-image generation with FLUX (B.8). These substantially broaden the represented data and task coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains Delta-DiT and T-GATE, and Table 4 retains Megatron-SP, DS-Ulysses, and DSP. WebVid extends the existing comparator set. The FLUX experiment uses the corresponding unaccelerated model as its control. Revised baseline hyperparameters concern experimental settings rather than comparator membership.

E3.justification: New protocols include WebVid comparisons against both ground-truth videos and original-model outputs, seven-dimension aggregation for the long-scene evaluation, and computation/communication isolation controls. Existing reported settings also change: Delta-DiT block ranges become [0,1] instead of [0,2] for Open-Sora-Plan and [0,2] instead of [0,5] for Latte; T-GATE's Open-Sora-Plan cache interval changes from 6 to 3. Table 4's stated duration changes from 2s to 8s. These revisions do not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 substantially extends the retained ablations with MLP analyses across layers and timesteps (Figures 13-15), complex-scene robustness tests (Table 11/Figure 16), separate computation and communication contributions (Table 12), operation-level attention profiling (Tables 13-15), and alternative redundancy measures (Figure 17). Figure 10 removes the 2s 480p multi-GPU scaling panel.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The added curves and tables do not introduce uncertainty reporting; attention-output variance concerns redundancy rather than statistical reliability.

E6.justification: Table 1's numerical results are identical, but v2 adds extensive appendix outcomes, including WebVid scores, seven-dimension long-video totals of 73.98 for PAB246 versus 74.54 for the original model, and FLUX latency of 7.8s versus 13.8s. Figure 7/Table 4 revise PAB's single-GPU Open-Sora latency from 71.25s to 73.25s, already shown in v1's Figure 10. Figure 10 also revises 1080p speedup annotations and removes the 2s 480p scaling results.

T1.justification: The diffusion equations, attention-broadcast formulation, and PSNR/LPIPS/SSIM formulas remain unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs. The added workflow illustrations and empirical redundancy metrics introduce no substantive mathematical derivation.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains training-free PAB with broadcast sequence parallelism. The introduction removes its claim about broadcasting diffusion steps and changes the highlighted generation rate from 20.6 to 35.6 FPS. The latter uses the 35.56 FPS result already present in v1's Figure 9, rather than establishing a new performance result.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations for MLP reuse based on periodic output-difference peaks and lower-layer stability, and attributes attention-module bottlenecks to the GPU behavior of normalization and positional embedding operations. It also interprets the new long-scene results as evidence of reliability under demanding conditions. The existing limitations concerning scene complexity and fixed broadcast strategies remain.

D1.justification: v1 omits exact PAB execution schedules. v2 identifies model versions, lists scheduler configurations, specifies attention-broadcast timestep windows, and supplies MLP block indices, broadcast timesteps, and reuse ranges in Tables 5-7. These materially improve implementation documentation without establishing a method change. Hardware, FlashAttention usage, and the code-access reference remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations for PyTorch 2, the WebVid source, and VideoLLM-online, while removing CogVideoX and several historical video-generation references. Section 4 refines discussion of caching and parallelism, but retains the central positioning around training-free acceleration of video DiTs and the same principal competing methods.

P1.justification: v2 condenses and rewrites related work into scheduler, compression, caching, and parallelism paragraphs, trims preliminaries, and makes local language and affiliation edits. It adds appendix navigation, moves metric descriptions after generation settings, and separates future work. The main narrative and section sequence remain largely intact.

P2.justification: New configuration/result tables and Figures 13-18 substantially expand the visual presentation. Existing displays are also revised: Figure 4(b) changes from bars to a numerical table, Figure 4(c) changes axes and curves, Table 2 adds colored differences, and Figure 10 reorders panels and removes one. Figure 11 is relocated, while the Figure 12 examples are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important reproducibility gap by specifying PAB's attention and MLP schedules. WebVid evaluation, demanding-scene tests, and computation/communication controls also substantially strengthen the empirical support. Reporting weaknesses remain: baseline-parameter revisions lack explanation, and Appendix B.4 describes a 24% latency reduction where Table 12 implies about 19%. These localized issues do not outweigh the substantial gains in reproducibility and experimental substantiation.
